Memory reduction reached at least 6x relative to uncompressed 16-bit KV storage. [...] KV cache quantization (TurboQuant, KIVI, SnapKV) compresses the dynamic state that grows during generation. Every new token adds to the cache, and compression must happen online, in real time, without seeing future tokens.

The technology could lower AI operational costs, enabling new use cases and driving exponential growth in total AI demand, paradoxically increasing overall memory requirements. results.title: TurboQuant: the new(?) and controversial ground breaking compression breakthrough from Google
results.content:
The key-value (KV) cache is the memory structure that allows transformer models to “remember” everything they’ve seen in a conversation or document during inference. Without it, the model would have to reprocess the entire context from scratch on every token generation step. The problem is architectural and unforgiving: KV cache memory grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size, which means serving real users at scale pushes it past comfortable limits fast. [...] TurboQuant KV cache compression targets exactly this bottleneck, which is why the research got immediate attention from practitioners who have been living inside this constraint for years. The promise of AI memory quantization that doesn’t compromise output quality is one of the most commercially valuable things a research team could deliver right now.

### What Google claims TurboQuant actually does [...] TurboQuant’s core mechanism applies quantization to KV cache tensors during inference, compressing the floating-point representations from 16-bit (BF16 or FP16) down to as low as 3 bits per value. The “Turbo” in the name refers to a novel transform applied to the KV cache tensors before quantization, the authors argue this transform smooths the distribution of values, making them more amenable to aggressive compression without the rounding errors that normally cause quality degradation.
